clue.text: Criticise grasping wife and weak man

indicators.note: to grasp something is to hold it tight, so one piece closes around another

parts.note: to pan a show is to criticise it harshly
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a henpecked husband, mocking both him and the wife who holds the reins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weak man' reads as a feeble husband, but it is the chess piece and, figuratively, a person used by others.
explanation.definitionFit: A pawn is the least powerful chess piece, and figuratively a person manipulated by stronger players.

clue.text: One group performing in desert

parts.note: one, as the indefinite article
a band is a group of musicians or people
a performer is on, as in on stage

explanation.surface: A lone band plays a concert out in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' looks like a sandy place where the band is playing, but it is the verb meaning to leave behind.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert someone is to leave them for good, which is exactly what abandoning means.

clue.text: Sensation created by this boldness

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the thing, not a synonym
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the fibre in the body that carries feeling to the brain

explanation.walkthrough: The first half describes the body's sensory fibre by what it does; the second is the everyday sense of audacity, as in 'what a nerve'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerves transmit physical feeling, and having the nerve to do something means having courage or cheek.

clue.text: Disapproving response securing end of rubbish comprehensive

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast inside, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a catcall is a jeering whistle or shout of disapproval

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: An audience jeers at a show it considers complete rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The jeer opens after its first four letters to take in one letter, giving CATCH-ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch-all category or term covers every case, so it is all-embracing or comprehensive.

clue.text: Constant effort required to turn part of machine

parts.note: c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to have a go is to make an effort or attempt

explanation.surface: Steady effort is needed to make a stiff machine part rotate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' fits the machinery picture, which hides that it reverses the effort.
explanation.definitionFit: A cog is a toothed wheel or tooth on a gear, a component inside machinery.

clue.text: Fairly good label tore unexpectedly

indicators.note: what happens unexpectedly does not go as planned, so the order of the letters is not kept

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A decent label ripped without warning as it was being peeled off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fairly good' sounds like a verdict on the label, but it is the definition standing apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerable describes something passable or acceptable, decent without being excellent.

clue.text: Arrangement of straps has to restrain drinkers regularly

indicators.note: restraining means holding something in check, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A bouncer's kit of straps is used to hold back rowdy drinkers at the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of the drinkers sit between the H-A and the S of 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: A harness is a set of straps fitted to a horse or person to control or secure them.

clue.text: What may scrub answer idiot brought up?

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing something up lifts it from bottom to top, so it reads backwards

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
a fool is an idiot

explanation.surface: A question about what might wipe out the reply some fool raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrub' suggests deleting or cancelling the answer, but here it means scouring in the bath.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofa is the dried fibrous fruit used as a bath sponge for scouring skin.

clue.text: Angry girl upset about a song

parts.note: mad means angry

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another
something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A furious girl is upset over a particular song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' doubles as the girl's mood; it shuffles her letters, which then go around the A.
explanation.definitionFit: A madrigal is a part-song for several unaccompanied voices, popular in the Renaissance.

clue.text: Bird caught by escaping criminal

indicators.note: something escaping gets away and is no longer there, so it is removed

parts.note: a crook is a criminal
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A bird gets snatched up by a fleeing lawbreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the bird caught; in the wordplay it is the abbreviation for 'caught' that escapes from the criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: The rook is a black crow-family bird that nests in colonies called rookeries.

clue.text: Advantage, for instance, of French revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning right round, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: eg is the abbreviation for 'for example'
de is French for 'of'

explanation.surface: A political point about the benefits of being a French revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' conjures the French Revolution but it reverses everything before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To have the edge over a rival is to hold a slight advantage over them.

clue.text: Standard means for processing cheese

parts.note: par is the standard or normal level

indicators.note: material sent for processing is broken down and reworked, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Describes the usual factory method for producing processed cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Processing' fits a cheese factory, which hides its role as the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Parmesan is a hard Italian cheese, an example of the general category named in the clue.

clue.text: Aristocratic Irishman snubbed Scotsman

indicators.note: to snub originally meant to cut short, so the last letter is removed

parts.note: Patrick, a typical Irish name, cut short
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: A snooty Irish nobleman cold-shoulders a man from Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snubbed' reads as a social slight, but it docks the Irishman's name; crosswords treat Pat, Patrick or Mick as stock Irishmen and Ian as a stock Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: Patricians were the hereditary noble class of ancient Rome, so the word describes aristocratic people or manners.

clue.text: Who fought in the dark reportedly?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a person, not a noun synonym

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so it is the sound that counts

parts.note: the dark is the night

explanation.surface: A question about who battled under cover of darkness.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K means the armoured warrior and the dark hours are pronounced identically.
explanation.definitionFit: Knights were mounted armoured warriors who fought for their lord in medieval times.

clue.text: Worker starts to get really behind

indicators.note: the start of each word is its first letter, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the first letters of the two words
behind in time or order means after

explanation.surface: An employee begins to fall seriously behind with the work.
explanation.walkthrough: Graft is British slang for hard work, so a grafter is a hard worker.
explanation.definitionFit: A grafter, in British informal use, is someone who works hard and diligently.

clue.text: Cleric somewhat entertained by dance

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken in, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: to bop is to dance
the suffix -ish means somewhat, and is used as a word on its own

explanation.surface: A clergyman is rather amused by a dance performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' is not a qualifier on 'entertained'; it is the casual word ish, as in 'it's ish'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop is a senior member of the clergy overseeing a diocese, a kind of cleric.

clue.text: Circular letter helping speech

parts.note: O is the round letter
a ration is a helping or portion

explanation.surface: An office memo sent round to all staff assists with a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circular letter' looks like a mailshot; it is the letter shaped like a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: An oration is a formal speech delivered on a ceremonial occasion.

clue.text: Level with peer that is bored by society

parts.note: a peer is one's equal

indicators.note: something bored by a drill has a hole made into it, so a piece is set inside it

parts.note: ie is the abbreviation for 'that is'
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: Speaking frankly with a member of the House of Lords who finds high society tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' suggests a lord, and 'bored' suggests tedium; in a British sense a peer is a noble, but here it is simply one's equal.
explanation.definitionFit: To level a score or contest is to make it even, which is what equalising means.

clue.text: Tom's partner belongs to baroque ensemble

indicators.note: what belongs to something is part of it, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A musician's companion plays in an early-music group.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom is not a person: a tom is a male cat, and a female cat is called a queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Among cats, the male is a tom and the female a queen, so she is the tom's mate.

clue.text: Plans to return unwanted correspondence

indicators.note: returning means going back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: maps are plans or charts

explanation.surface: Someone intends to send back letters they never wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plans' reads as a verb about intentions; it is the noun for drawings or charts.
explanation.definitionFit: Spam is junk email, unsolicited messages sent in bulk that nobody asked for.

clue.text: Criticism of branch with little substance?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a thin piece of wood from a tree

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a branch of study as lacking any real content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting stick' is British informal for being criticised; the second half is a jokey picture of a slender twig.
explanation.definitionFit: Stick is informal British for criticism, and also a thin, insubstantial length of wood from a tree.

clue.text: Support others

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a prop on which something is laid, as in an armrest

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase it sounds like an instruction to help other people; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A rest is a device that supports something, and 'the rest' means the remaining ones or others.

clue.text: Understood simplicity has no limits

indicators.note: a word without limits loses its boundaries, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A philosophical remark that being simple can be endless yet clear.
explanation.walkthrough: Stripping the first and last letters from the ten-letter word leaves eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something implicit is understood without being stated outright, implied rather than expressed.

clue.text: Writer of verse, for the most part?

indicators.note: most but not all of something is kept, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a poem is a piece of verse

explanation.surface: Asking whether an author mostly wrote poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Allan Poe wrote both stories and poems, so the surface question is apt: he was a writer of verse for part of his output.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Allan Poe was an American author of short stories and poems such as The Raven.

clue.text: Charm of actor's appearance on stage

definitions.meaning: first meaning, stressed on the second syllable: to enchant or delight
second meaning, stressed on the first syllable: the act of coming on

explanation.surface: Praising the magnetism of a performer as they walk on.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are spelt the same but said differently: en-TRANCE to bewitch, EN-trance for coming in.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to cast a spell over them, and an actor's entrance is their arrival on stage.

clue.text: Royal family meeting head of government

parts.note: kin are one's family

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The royal household holds a meeting with the prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal family' looks like one phrase but splits: the first word is the definition, used as a noun for a member of royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: A king is a male monarch, the most senior member of a royal house.
